name: tutorial_lobbying_triage
document:
# Tutorial: Lobbying Say-versus-Do (deliberately artificial sample)

## Purpose

A lobbying filing says what an organisation paid to ask government for. A public
commitment says what that same organisation told everyone else it would do. Reporting in
this genre is almost always the join of the two: the lead is not a filing on its own, it
is a filing that asks for the opposite of what its client promised in public. This
five-step tutorial workflow joins each filing to its client's public commitment and flags
the pairs that contradict.

The sample data is INVENTED. Every organisation is fictional, nothing is fetched from the
network, and no row describes a real filing, client, firm or commitment.

## Input data

Two bundled CSVs.

`tutorial_lobbying_triage.csv`, one row per filing:

- `filing_id` — stable, unique identifier for the filing
- `client` — the organisation that retained the lobbyists
- `registrant` — the lobbying firm that filed the disclosure
- `amount_usd` — reported lobbying spend for the period, in whole US dollars
- `filing_period` — the reporting period, e.g. "2024 Q1"
- `specific_issues` — the filer's own one-line account of what this filing asked for

`tutorial_public_commitments.csv`, one row per organisation:

- `client` — the organisation that made the commitment
- `public_commitment` — one line of what it said in public it would do
- `commitment_source` — where it said it, e.g. "2023 climate pledge"

## Step 1 — Join each filing to its client's public commitment

Bring `public_commitment` and `commitment_source` onto every filing, matched on
the client name. This is a many-to-one join: the commitments file carries at most one row
per organisation, and a repeat would fail the run rather than quietly multiply filings.
No filing is dropped here. A filing whose client has no commitment row keeps every one of
its own fields and carries a blank commitment — the absence is the record, and the next
step is told to read it as an absence rather than as a judgment.

## Step 2 — Judge the filing against the commitment (LLM)

For each filing, read the client's public commitment and this filing's ask together, and
add two fields — one filing in, one filing out (the filing is neither dropped nor duplicated):

- `alignment` — one of: Contradicts, Matches, Unclear, No commitment given. "Contradicts"
  means this filing asks government for the opposite of what the client committed to.
  "No commitment given" is the answer when the commitment field is blank.
- `alignment_note` — a single plain sentence naming what the client said and what this
  filing asks for.

The model is given only these two texts, and is told not to use anything it knows about
the organisation and not to invent a commitment that is not in front of it. Filings are
read twelve at a time in one model call.

## Step 3 — Flag the contradictions

Add `contradicts_commitment`, decided in plain code from two fields and nothing else: a
filing contradicts when a commitment was actually joined onto it AND `alignment` reads
"Contradicts". A filing with no commitment on record is never flagged — there is nothing
for it to contradict, and the code decides that, not the model. A filing that has a
commitment but no judgment is not guessed either — the step stops and says which filing
it was.

## Step 4 — Publish the report

Produce a single HTML page listing every filing with client, registrant,
reported spend, what the filing asked for, what the client committed to in public (or that
no commitment is on record), and the model's judgment. A flagged filing also shows both
sides side by side — the commitment as said, and the ask as filed — so the page carries
the contradiction itself rather than a bare flag. No score, no ranking and no
recommendation: the report is a reading aid, not a verdict.

Every row also carries a link back to that row's lineage — each stage that touched it, back
to the input row it came from — so a reader can check any line of the page against the run.

The page's markup and stylesheet are a committed template file, not text assembled inside
the step; the step fills its placeholders and writes the result.

## Out of scope

No external fetching, no human-review queue, no filtering, and no second join — one join,
one model read, one flag, one page.

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are checking one lobbying filing against what the same organisation has said in public.

Return a JSON object with exactly these two fields:

1. "alignment": exactly one of — Contradicts | Matches | Unclear | No commitment given
   - "Contradicts": the filing asks government for the opposite of what the commitment says.
   - "Matches": the filing asks government for what the commitment says.
   - "Unclear": the two texts are about different things, or neither supports nor conflicts with the other.
   - "No commitment given": the commitment line is blank, or reads `nan` or `None` because no commitment was on record for that organisation. Answer this and nothing else in that case — do not judge, and do not supply a commitment yourself.

2. "alignment_note": one plain sentence naming what the organisation said in public and what this filing asks for. Empty string when there is no commitment to compare against.

Judge only the two texts in front of you. Do not use anything you know or believe about the organisation, and never invent, complete or paraphrase a commitment that is not printed here.

stages.description: Flag filings that contradict their client's public commitment
compiler_notes: Decided from the joined commitment and the model's alignment alone — no spend, no re-reading of either text.
The no-commitment case is settled in code, not by the model: an absent commitment is never a contradiction, whatever the model answered for that row.

adds.name: contradicts_commitment
adds.description: True when a public commitment was joined onto this filing and the model judged the filing's ask to contradict it.

function.summary: Flags a filing when a public commitment was joined onto it AND the model judged its ask to contradict that commitment. A filing with no commitment on record is never flagged — there is nothing for it to contradict. A filing that has a commitment but no judgment is not guessed; the step stops and says which filing it was.

corner_cases.case: a filing carries a commitment and `alignment` is `Contradicts`
a filing carries a commitment and `alignment` is `Matches`
corner_cases.expected: the filing is kept and not flagged

corner_cases.case: the join matched no commitment, so `public_commitment` is blank
corner_cases.expected: the filing is kept and not flagged, whatever `alignment` says

corner_cases.case: a filing carries a commitment but `alignment` is blank
corner_cases.expected: the step fails, naming the filing, rather than flagging it either way

compiler_notes: The document says this is a reading aid, not a verdict — no score, ranking or recommendation column is rendered. A flagged row shows the two texts the flag was decided from and adds nothing.
A filing flagged as contradicting a commitment the join never matched stops the step: the page must not show a contradiction it cannot print both sides of.
A filing with no commitment on record says so in its own cell rather than rendering an empty one, so the join's non-matches are visible on the page and not just in lineage.

The report's markup and stylesheet are the committed file app/seeds/data/tutorial_triage_report.html; TEMPLATE_PATH is bound to it when the tutorial project is seeded, the way the input CSV paths are. A missing file or a missing section stops the step rather than publishing a half-rendered page.
This stage writes the HTML to disk and returns a file-path pointer rather than embedding the markup inline, which is practical at scale.

function.summary: Fills the committed report template — one row per filing, in the order they arrived — with the reported spend, what the filing asked for, what the client committed to in public or that no commitment is on record, the model's judgment, and for a flagged filing both texts side by side.

corner_cases.expected: the step fails, naming the file, rather than writing a partial page
